offered_action_specs.name: rollback_deploy
offered_action_specs.description: Roll one service back to the settings it ran before its latest deploy, as the deploy log records them. Code plans it from that log, not from your tools' results, so you can name it even when they cannot see deploys: if the log holds no deploy of that service to undo, or the service changed since, code refuses it. Its container is recreated, so the service pauses while it restarts. Money already booked wrong stays wrong: a rollback stops new damage, and repairs nothing.

proposed.why: Deploy timing, receiver logs and webhook metrics all point to the same cause, so I am confident enough to diagnose.

diagnosis.hypothesis: webhook-receiver was redeployed at 21:20:02 with WEBHOOK_SECRET_VERSION=v2. The provider still signs webhooks with the old secret, so the receiver now fails every signature check and answers 400 'webhook refused: bad signature'. Nothing is acknowledged or put on provider-events after that. The provider keeps resending, so the backlog of unacknowledged webhooks grows (133 at the alert, 21:20:50) and the money check cannot settle up to its cutoff. The total webhook rate is climbing because the same refused webhooks come back as retries, not because real traffic grew.

evidence.shows: webhook-receiver is the newest deploy, at 21:20:02, with WEBHOOK_SECRET_VERSION=v2. That is 48 s before the alert. All other services were deployed at 21:18:36 and have not changed since.
Every recent webhook-receiver log line on /webhooks/provider is status 400 with 'webhook refused: bad signature', reason 'signature mismatch'.
Before 21:20 every webhook was 'queued'. 'bad_signature' first appears at 21:20:19 and climbs to about 19/s, while 'queued' falls toward zero by 21:20:34. The switch follows the deploy.
The total webhook rate rises from about 4/s to about 19/s after the deploy. This fits the provider resending refused webhooks.

proposed_fix.summary: Roll webhook-receiver back to the settings it ran before the 21:20:02 deploy, which should be the previous secret version that matches the provider's signing key. The provider's retries should then be accepted and queued, and the backlog should drain. Afterwards, run money_check with wait=true to confirm the books caught up. If v2 is wanted, rotate it in coordination with the provider, or have the receiver accept both versions during the switch.

diagnosis.blast_radius: Only webhook-receiver is recreated, so it pauses briefly. Webhooks sent during the pause get no acknowledgement and the provider resends them, so nothing is lost. When the backlog drains, the consumers get a burst of events. ledger-consumer runs the idempotent handler and payment-confirmer looks events up by our id, so duplicate deliveries should not double-book. This is not verified here. Not checked: whether v2 was meant as a coordinated key rotation that the provider will switch to soon. If so, a rollback would only delay the rotation.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: If the rollback makes things worse, for example if the provider has in fact moved to v2, redeploy webhook-receiver with WEBHOOK_SECRET_VERSION=v2. Then check the logs and the klaxon_webhooks_received_total result label to see whether 'queued' or 'bad_signature' dominates.
